title: 2 Chronicles
summary: 2 Chronicles is a biblical book focused on temple worship, royal faithfulness, exile, and restoration hope.
historical_context: Second Chronicles interprets Judah's monarchy through the temple, covenant response, exile, and the hope opened by Cyrus' decree.
ancient_near_east_context: 2 Chronicles belongs to the ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern world reflected in its setting, institutions, and canonical placement.
hebraic_worldview: 2 Chronicles should be read with attention to covenant memory, communal identity, worship, wisdom, and accountability before the Lord.
second_temple_context: Second Temple readers received 2 Chronicles as part of Israel's Scriptures and read it within questions of identity, worship, exile, and hope.
canonical_context: Within Historical Books, book 9 of 12, 2 Chronicles contributes to the Bible's unfolding witness by connecting temple worship, royal faithfulness, exile, and restoration hope to the larger storyline.
later_christian_reception: Christian interpretation has read 2 Chronicles as part of the canonical witness to faithfulness, judgment, mercy, and hope in Christ-centered Scripture reading.
literary_context: 2 Chronicles uses narrative within Historical Books, book 9 of 12 to develop its themes through the book's structure and key passages.
covenantal_significance: 2 Chronicles helps readers trace covenant faithfulness, failure, mercy, and hope within its canonical setting.
authorship_positions: Many scholars read the books as later historiographical or Deuteronomistic shaping
date_ranges: Historical span from settlement through exile
Final form often placed in the exilic or post-exilic period
original_audience: Israel and Judah remembering the land, monarchy, and exile
historical_setting: Settlement, monarchy, and exile in the land of Israel and Judah
canonical_role: 2 Chronicles anchors temple worship, royal faithfulness, exile, and restoration hope within Historical Books, book 9 of 12 and connects the book to related people, places, events, and themes.
interpretive_disputes: How conquest, kingship, and exile are narrated theologically

related_objects.notes: Solomon and the temple dominate the opening movement.
Temple worship remains the main theological center.
Jerusalem is the royal and temple city.
The exile marks the book's covenant crisis.
The closing decree points toward restoration after exile.
